tagline.text: A small island of white sand and a lighthouse off Matalom

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May dry season (clear weather lasts into June–early July)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,000 (per person, day trip from Matalom including entrance fee, boat and meals; lodging and transport extra)

children.text: Canigao Island is a small uninhabited island off Matalom in Leyte, reached from Matalom port by boat in
15–30 minutes
. It has a white sand beach, a sandbar and a small lighthouse, and the entrance fee plus boat fare come to only about
, so it is an easy and affordable trip.

Canigao Island lies off Matalom on the southwest coast of Leyte, where the Camotes Sea, the Canigao Channel and the Bohol Sea meet. Wikipedia describes it as an uninhabited island whose only notable man-made structure is a lighthouse. It sits at roughly 10.248° N, 124.750° E, and from Matalom port it is clearly visible just offshore. On the map it lies in the narrow strait between Bohol and Leyte, and on a clear day you can see neighboring islands in the distance.
The appeal of the island is its simplicity. Many travelers say a slow walk around it takes only
15–30 minutes
, the main beach is about
long, and the sandbar extending from one end is described as about

. Palm trees and shady woods make it easy to hang a hammock and relax, and the area around the lighthouse and the rocky stretches are good for photos. It is not as crowded as Boracay or Balicasag in Bohol, and reviewers keep noting that weekdays are quiet. On weekends and holidays, however, crowds arrive and the shared grill area can get busy.

The island is managed by the Matalom local government, with an entrance fee, a boat fare and zones restricted to protect the environment. The western and northern parts are a nature sanctuary, and swimming, diving, fishing, snorkeling and boating there are said to be restricted by law. Some travelers report seeing sharks and tropical fish in the fish sanctuary, but you should ask locals or staff first how far you may go.

Canigao Island alone is enough for a half-day trip, but combining it with other sights around Matalom makes for a full day. A common plan is to visit Hitoog Cave or Karap-agan (Mahayahay) Falls in the morning and cross to the island in the afternoon. Along the southwestern coast of Leyte, small islands such as Kalanggaman Island and Cuatro Islas form an island-hopping route, and many travelers add Canigao as one stop. The information below draws on 2016–2025 travel reports and wiki sources; fees and the departure port can change, so check with the Matalom local government before you go.
The heart of the island is a white sand beach about

long. The water is clear and shallow in many places, good for swimming and sunbathing, with neighboring islands visible in the distance. Open cottages and shops cluster on the east side of the beach, right where the boat lands.
A sandbar about

long extends from one side of the beach and can be reached on foot. With sea on both sides it is considered a photo highlight, and its shape changes with the tide, so your feet may get wet at high tide.

The most prominent man-made structure on the island is the lighthouse. The area around it and the rocky stretches are good for landscape photos, and reviews also mention a viewing cottage and a path among the rocks. The rocks can be slippery, so water shoes are more comfortable than sandals.

Part of the island is a marine sanctuary said to be rich in tropical fish and coral. Reviewers say there is no snorkel gear for rent on the island, so bring your own mask and snorkel. Swimming and fishing inside the sanctuary may be restricted, and touching coral or taking marine life is prohibited.

The woods on the west side of the island are said to be home to wild monkeys, and there are plenty of trees for hanging a hammock. Even when the area near the landing is busy, the far side of the island stays quiet, making it a good place to read or nap.
You can bring or rent a tent and camp overnight. The tent pitching fee is listed at
(one report says
in the off-season). The stars, sunrise and sunset are all part of the appeal, but electricity is limited, so bring a power bank and a flashlight.

A small shop on the island sells water, drinks, snacks and cooked meals. Fishermen sometimes sell their catch, and reviewers say you can order fresh shellfish and fish near the pier. Prices are described as reasonable compared with other tourist spots.

) and Karap-agan (Mahayahay) Falls can be reached by habal-habal (motorbike taxi) from Matalom town, and the falls reportedly have no entrance fee. Visit both in the morning and cross to the island in the afternoon for a full day.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: Cross from Matalom port to the island for half a day

children.text: Arrive near Matalom plaza. Many guides say the port is close to the plaza and can be reached on foot. Buy the boat ticket and entrance fee at the port.
The banca leaves once it is reasonably full. Service starts early in the morning and the crossing usually takes
15–30 minutes
. One traveler says the departure point has moved from Matalom to nearby Itum, so confirm the port location first.
On arrival, pay the entrance fee and claim a cottage or a shady spot. Drop your bags and look around the main beach and the sandbar first.
If you snorkel, do so in a permitted area outside the sanctuary, and get lunch and drinks at the shop.
Walk around the lighthouse, the rocky area and the woods on the far side. The island is small, so even a slow walk takes under
30 minutes
Pack up and return to the landing. The last boat from the island to the port is generally given as
, so leave yourself some margin.
If the weather is bad, boats may not run, so it is wise to keep a backup plan.

Reviews say Matalom has almost no lodging, so many travelers stay in Bato or Hilongos.

The dry season from March to May is said to be the best time for Canigao Island. The sea is calm and clear, which makes snorkeling and camping easier, and some guides say clear weather lasts into June and early July.

In the rainy season, wind and waves can cancel boats, and if you are staying overnight your departure may be delayed. The central Philippines is within the typhoon belt, so check the forecast and Matalom local government announcements before you go.

There are three ways to stay on the island: rent an open cottage on the beach (overnight about
), book a room (about
), or pitch a tent (about

). Rooms and bungalows are booked through the Matalom local government tourism office's Facebook page, but reviewers say replies are slow, so contact them early or ask at the office in person on the morning of your trip. Matalom town has few places to stay, so travelers who want to sleep in town book lodging in Bato or Hilongos instead.

The island has a small shop selling water, drinks, snacks and simple meals, but the menu is limited, so bring plenty of food and water. A shared grill is available for campers, so bring cooking gear. Fresh seafood is sometimes brought by fishermen or bought at the market near the pier and grilled on site. Shower and toilet water is brackish, so soap may not lather well.
Bring your own mask, snorkel and water shoes. Many reviews say there is no rental gear on the island.
For a day trip, leave early to avoid rushing. Plan around the last boat back, which is generally given as about
Bring drinking water, snacks, sunscreen, a hat, sunglasses and a power bank, and carry plenty of cash. Do not count on cards or electronic payments.
Mobile phones mostly get a signal, though it can be weak in places. Electricity is limited, so charge your devices beforehand.
If you bring a hammock, the shady woods on the island are a good place to rest. Even when the landing area is busy, the far side of the island stays quiet.
Take your trash back with you whenever possible, and do not step on or touch the coral.
Reviews mention sea urchins, so wear shoes or water shoes when you go into the sea.
Port location and fees can change, so check with the Matalom local government or local residents first.
The western and northern parts of the island are a sanctuary where swimming, diving, fishing and snorkeling may be restricted, and catching or taking fish and marine life is prohibited.
Before entering the water, ask local staff or residents which areas are permitted.
Boats can be canceled in bad weather, so avoid scheduling the island right before a flight home.
Watch out for sea urchins and slippery rocks, and check that life jackets are available if you travel with children.
Reviewers doubt the quality of drinking water on the island, so bring bottled water.
Fees and the port location differ between reports, so confirm the latest information locally.
